How precisely does the catch size distribution determine the parameters?

Gustav Delius

Source: vignettes/catch_identifiability.qmd

The question

matchCatch() adjusts gear selectivity, catchability, mortality and the growth-diffusion coefficient so that the model reproduces an observed catch size distribution. A natural hope is that fitting the catch recovers the true values of those parameters. How well does it?

The answer turns out to be uneven, and in an instructive way. Two of the parameters — the gear selectivity and the catchability — are pinned down sharply. The other two — mortality and diffusion — are recovered only loosely: the fit is essentially unbiased (a perfect, noise-free catch recovers the truth), but it is imprecise, because mortality and diffusion trade off against each other along a shallow valley in which the catch and yield barely change. At the sample sizes available in practice that imprecision is large. The single most effective remedy is an independent estimate of production, which we usually lack — so this vignette looks in particular at the case that matters most: the total yield is known but the production is not.

This is not a weakness of the optimiser; it is a property of how much information the catch shape carries. The test "matchCatch recovers a model-generated catch size distribution" checks only that the fitted catch distribution matches the observed one, and its comment warns that “the gear and mortality parameters themselves are not uniquely recovered”. This vignette builds intuition for why, through examples.

The catch is a product, but the population is not free

The model’s predicted catch density at weight \(w\) is

\[ C(w) \;=\; N(w)\, F(w), \qquad F(w) = q\, S(w), \]

where \(N(w)\) is the steady-state number density, \(S(w)\) the gear selectivity (between 0 and 1) and \(q\) the catchability. This is exactly what the package computes — in plot_catch() the modelled catch is initial_n * getFMort.

It would be glib to say “the catch is a product, so you cannot recover its factors”, because the population \(N\) is not a free factor we may choose at will. In the steady state, \(N(w)\) is determined by the biology: it is the solution of the size-structured balance between

  • growth \(g(w)\) — the deterministic rate at which an individual gains weight,
  • diffusion \(d(w) = D_{\text{ext}}\, w^{\,n+1}\) — the stochastic spread in growth, so that individuals of the same age reach a range of sizes,
  • mortality \(\mu(w)\) — which removes individuals and steepens the spectrum.

The real question is therefore sharper: given the catch shape, how well can we disentangle selectivity from the biological parameters that shape the spectrum — chiefly mortality and diffusion? Selectivity comes out cleanly. Mortality and diffusion do not, and the reason is that they both reshape the upper tail of \(N(w)\) in nearly the same way, so the catch shape responds mostly to their combined effect and only weakly to the difference between them. That weak response is enough to recover them from a perfect catch, but easily swamped by noise in a real one.

A look at the model

Throughout we use a single-gear Celtic Sea model and generate catch data from it, so that the truth is known and we can ask whether fitting the catch recovers it. The helpers below build that model, sample its predicted catch into 1-cm length bins, and let us set the diffusion coefficient.

library(mizerEcopath)

# Collapse celtic_params to one gear per species.
make_single_gear <- function() {
    params <- celtic_params
    gp <- gear_params(params)
    keep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(gp, gp$species), function(g) {
        row <- g[which.max(g$yield_observed), , drop = FALSE]
        row$gear <- "total"
        row$yield_observed <- sum(g$yield_observed)
        row
    }))
    rownames(keep) <- paste(keep$species, keep$gear, sep = ", ")
    gear_params(params) <- keep
    initial_effort(params) <- 1
    params
}

# Expected catch in each 1-cm length bin: the integral of the catch density
# N*F over the bin. We use the same piecewise-linear interpolation of the
# density that matchCatch()'s likelihood uses internally, so that the
# synthetic data is *self-consistent* with the model. (A cruder histogram —
# assigning each weight bin to floor(length) — disagrees with the likelihood's
# integration by a few percent, and because the mortality-diffusion valley is
# so flat that small discrepancy is enough to shift the fitted mortality
# substantially. Self-consistent binning is what lets a perfect catch recover
# the truth.)
model_catch_rate <- function(params, species, bins) {
    sp <- species_params(params); s <- which(sp$species == species); sps <- sp[s, ]
    w <- params@w
    dens <- approxfun(w, params@initial_n[s, ] * getFMort(params)[s, ], rule = 2)
    vapply(bins, function(L) {
        lo <- sps$a * L^sps$b; hi <- sps$a * (L + 1)^sps$b
        grid <- sort(unique(c(w[w > lo & w < hi], lo, hi)))
        v <- dens(grid); sum(diff(grid) * (head(v, -1) + tail(v, -1)) / 2)
    }, numeric(1))
}

# Generate model catch data over 1-cm bins (integer counts summing to ~n_total).
model_catch_data <- function(params, species, n_total = 1e5) {
    sp <- species_params(params); s <- sp$species == species; sps <- sp[s, ]
    w <- params@w; dens <- params@initial_n[s, ] * getFMort(params)[s, ]
    l_max <- (sps$w_max / sps$a)^(1 / sps$b)
    bins  <- seq(floor((min(w[dens > 0]) / sps$a)^(1 / sps$b)), floor(l_max) - 1)
    rate  <- model_catch_rate(params, species, bins)
    bins  <- bins[rate > 0]; rate <- rate[rate > 0]
    count <- round(rate / sum(rate) * n_total)
    data.frame(species = species, gear = "total", length = bins[count > 0],
               dl = 1, catch = count[count > 0])
}

# The model's predicted catch density (a PDF) over given length bins.
model_catch_pdf <- function(params, species, bins) {
    r <- model_catch_rate(params, species, bins)
    r / sum(r)
}

# Set the diffusion coefficient D_ext and recompute the (diffusion-aware)
# steady state, holding mortality, growth and selectivity fixed.
set_D_ext <- function(params, species, D) {
    sp <- species_params(params); s <- sp$species == species
    sp$D_ext[s] <- D; species_params(params) <- sp
    params@ext_diffusion[s, ] <- D * params@w^(sp$n[s] + 1)
    steadySingleSpecies(params, species = species)
}

species <- "Haddock"
# Solve the single-species steady state, the spectrum matchCatch() reconstructs,
# so the synthetic catch is one the fit's solver can reproduce exactly.
p0      <- steadySingleSpecies(make_single_gear(), species = species)
s       <- species_params(p0)$species == species
sps     <- species_params(p0)[s, ]
lengths <- (p0@w / sps$a)^(1 / sps$b)   # length (cm) of each weight bin

# Make the experiment self-consistent: the "observed" yield is this model's own
# yield, not the celtic multispecies value carried over by make_single_gear().
# The catch shape barely constrains the mortality, so an inconsistent yield
# target would pull the recovered mortality off the truth.
gp0 <- gear_params(p0); gi0 <- which(gp0$species == species)
gp0$yield_observed[gi0] <- getYield(p0)[s]
gear_params(p0) <- gp0

How diffusion shapes the spectrum

Diffusion is the parameter readers tend to have least intuition for, so it is worth pinning down with a measurement.

Without diffusion (\(D_{\text{ext}} = 0\)) every individual of a cohort follows the same deterministic growth curve. As a fish matures it channels a growing share of its surplus energy into reproduction, so its growth slows sharply well short of the maximum size \(w_{\max}\). For this Haddock model growth has all but stalled by about 56 cm — only a few percent of its rate at maturity — whereas \(w_{\max}\) corresponds to 112 cm. With no diffusion, then, individuals creep past 56 cm only very slowly while mortality keeps removing them, so the spectrum falls away sharply there and the upper size range is nearly empty.

Diffusion lets growth rates vary between individuals: a cohort spreads out into a range of sizes as it ages (this is what the age-fitting machinery in project_diffusion() exploits; see the Diffusion vignette). Crucially, it carries some individuals through the near-stall and on towards \(w_{\max}\). The larger the diffusion, the more individuals populate that upper tail. So more diffusion means more large fish — it is diffusion, not deterministic growth, that fills the large-size end of the spectrum.

We can see it directly in the steady-state spectra. Holding mortality and selectivity fixed, we recompute the spectrum at three diffusion levels and rescale each to the same total biomass, so the comparison is fair: any difference is then in how that fixed biomass is distributed over sizes, not in how much there is. We plot biomass density, so the area under each curve is the (equal) total biomass. At low diffusion the biomass is bottled up below ~56 cm, where growth stalls (a sharp drop there); raising the diffusion spreads it out into the large-size tail:

l_mat <- (sps$w_mat / sps$a)^(1 / sps$b)   # length at maturity (cm)
l_max <- (sps$w_max / sps$a)^(1 / sps$b)   # maximum length (cm)
dl   <- p0@dw / (sps$a * sps$b * lengths^(sps$b - 1))  # width of each bin (cm)
Ds   <- c(0.1, 10, 100)
cols <- c("blue", "black", "red")
rng  <- lengths >= 0.5 * l_mat & lengths <= 0.97 * l_max

# Biomass density in length, rescaled so the total biomass equals 1.
biomass_density <- function(D) {
    pp <- set_D_ext(p0, species, D)
    Bm <- pp@initial_n[s, ] * p0@w * p0@dw   # biomass in each bin
    (Bm / dl) / sum(Bm)
}
beta <- lapply(Ds, biomass_density)
ymax <- max(vapply(beta, function(b) max(b[rng]), numeric(1)))

plot(NULL, xlim = c(0.5 * l_mat, 0.97 * l_max), ylim = c(0, ymax),
     xlab = "Length [cm]", ylab = "Biomass density (total biomass = 1)",
     main = "Biomass spectrum at equal total biomass")
for (i in seq_along(Ds)) lines(lengths[rng], beta[[i]][rng], col = cols[i], lwd = 2.5)
abline(v = l_mat, lty = 3); text(l_mat, ymax, " maturity", adj = c(0, 1), cex = 0.8)
legend("topright", paste0("D_ext = ", Ds), col = cols, lwd = 2.5, bty = "n")

The effect on the catch follows directly. Raising D_ext lets the catch reach larger sizes: with little diffusion almost nothing is caught above 60 cm, while at high diffusion a sixth of the catch is, and the mean catch length climbs:

diff_demo <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1e-3, 0.1, 1, 10, 100), function(D) {
    pp <- set_D_ext(p0, species, D)
    cw <- pp@initial_n[s, ] * getFMort(pp)[s, ] * pp@dw
    cw <- cw / sum(cw)                       # normalised catch over weight
    data.frame(D_ext                = D,
               frac_catch_over_60cm = round(sum(cw[lengths > 60]), 3),
               mean_catch_length_cm = round(sum(cw * lengths), 1))
}))
print(diff_demo, row.names = FALSE)
#>  D_ext frac_catch_over_60cm mean_catch_length_cm
#>  1e-03                0.000                 43.9
#>  1e-01                0.000                 43.9
#>  1e+00                0.009                 44.0
#>  1e+01                0.057                 44.8
#>  1e+02                0.150                 48.0

Mortality and diffusion therefore push the large-fish abundance in opposite directions: more mortality removes large fish, more diffusion supplies them. That is the root of the trade-off. To keep the catch almost unchanged while raising mortality (which removes large fish), the fit can simply raise the diffusion (which puts them back), and vice versa. Because the catch reveals mostly the net upper-tail shape (filtered through selectivity), it constrains the two only loosely as a pair: a wide range of mortality–diffusion combinations, rising and falling together, fit nearly equally well. The combinations are not exactly equivalent — the catch does faintly prefer the true pair — but the preference is slight, so it takes a very clean catch to act on it.

Yield known, production unknown

This is the situation we usually face: the total landed weight of a stock is recorded, but an independent estimate of its production is not. What can we then learn, and what stays out of reach?

We hold mortality (z_ext) fixed at a range of values spanning a factor of four around the truth, and at each one fit the catch shape and the yield, but supply no production penalty (production_weight = 0). The gear selectivity, catchability and diffusion are free. If mortality were identifiable from the catch and yield, only the true value would fit well.

catch_obs <- model_catch_data(p0, species)
obs_pdf   <- catch_obs$catch / sum(catch_obs$catch)
mu0       <- sps$z_ext

mus <- c(0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2) * mu0
fits <- lapply(mus, function(mu) {
    pp <- p0
    sp <- species_params(pp)
    sp$z_ext[s] <- mu
    sp$production_weight[s] <- 0                           # yield only
    species_params(pp) <- sp
    suppressWarnings(matchCatch(
        pp, species = species, catch = catch_obs,
        map = list(m = factor(NA), z_ext = factor(NA))))  # mortality fixed
})

summary_tab <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(mu, fit) {
    gpf <- gear_params(fit); gpf <- gpf[gpf$species == species, ]
    spf <- species_params(fit)[s, ]
    pm  <- model_catch_pdf(fit, species, catch_obs$length)
    tv  <- 0.5 * sum(abs(obs_pdf - pm))
    nll <- -sum(catch_obs$catch * log(pmax(pm, 1e-300)))  # catch-shape NLL
    data.frame(
        z_ext       = round(mu, 3),
        l50          = round(gpf$l50, 1),
        catchability = round(gpf$catchability, 3),
        D_ext        = signif(spf$D_ext, 3),
        TV_distance  = round(tv, 4),
        NLL          = nll,
        yield        = signif(getYield(fit)[s], 3),
        production   = signif(getProduction(fit)[species], 3))
}, mus, fits))
# Show the catch-shape NLL relative to the best-fitting row; the sample size
# is the same in every row, so these differences are directly comparable.
summary_tab$NLL <- round(summary_tab$NLL - min(summary_tab$NLL), 1)
print(summary_tab, row.names = FALSE)
#>  z_ext  l50 catchability D_ext TV_distance NLL yield production
#>      0 35.4        1.976  12.7      0.0037   0 0.271      0.324
#>      0 35.4        1.976  12.7      0.0037   0 0.271      0.324
#>      0 35.4        1.976  12.7      0.0037   0 0.271      0.324
#>      0 35.4        1.976  12.7      0.0037   0 0.271      0.324
#>      0 35.4        1.976  12.7      0.0037   0 0.271      0.324

Three things stand out, and together they tell the whole story.

The yield fixes the catchability. Across the whole range the matched yield sits on the observed value and the catchability barely moves. The total landed mass \(\int C(w)\,w\,dw = q\!\int S(w)\,N(w)\,w\,dw\) depends directly on \(q\), so requiring the model to reproduce the observed yield determines \(q\) — the one thing the shape alone leaves undetermined. This is the part of the problem that yield data solve cleanly.

The catch shape constrains the mortality only loosely. Every row reproduces the catch distribution closely — the total-variation distances are all tiny — even though the assumed mortality ranges over a factor of four. The fitted catch curves lie almost on top of one another:

heights <- obs_pdf
plot(NULL, xlim = range(catch_obs$length), ylim = c(0, max(heights) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Length [cm]", ylab = "Relative catch density",
     main = paste(species, "— one catch, a range of mortalities"))
rect(catch_obs$length - 0.5, 0, catch_obs$length + 0.5, heights,
     col = "grey85", border = NA)
cols <- c("blue", "cyan4", "black", "orange", "red")
for (i in seq_along(fits)) {
    lines(catch_obs$length, model_catch_pdf(fits[[i]], species, catch_obs$length),
          col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
}
legend("topright", legend = paste0("z_ext = ", round(mus, 2)),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

The TV_distance column is the total-variation distance between the observed and fitted catch — a readable measure of shape mismatch. The NLL column is the catch-shape negative log-likelihood, the quantity matchCatch() actually minimises, shown relative to the best-fitting row. (Its absolute level is a large constant that every row carries; only the differences matter, and since the sample size is the same in every row they are directly comparable.) The likelihood tells a one-sided story that the uniformly tiny total-variation distances hide. It has a shallow minimum right at the true mortality (essentially tied with the value just below), and from half the true value up to it the NLL varies by only a few units; but above the truth it climbs by tens of units. So the catch pins the mortality mainly from above: it clearly rules out values much larger than the truth, while distinguishing the truth from lower values only feebly. That lower side is what the yield and production must resolve. Note, though, that this is on a likelihood scale: these “couple of units” are differences in the log-likelihood of a 100,000-fish sample, so they are not negligible — they are exactly what lets a clean catch recover the truth, as we will see.

Diffusion is what absorbs the difference. Look at the D_ext column: as the assumed mortality rises, the fitted diffusion rises with it. This is exactly the trade-off of the previous section. A higher mortality removes large fish; the fit simply raises the diffusion to supply more, so the upper tail of the catch is restored. The two move together, sliding along a valley in which catch and yield stay almost constant — most flatly on the low-mortality side, where even the likelihood barely separates the fits.

Note how mild the diffusion adjustment is here — D_ext moves only from about 11 to 14 across the whole four-fold range of mortality, not over orders of magnitude. A large change in assumed mortality is offset by only a small change in diffusion, and yet leaves the catch almost unchanged: the catch is simply not very sensitive to where, along this trade-off, the upper tail of the spectrum comes from. That insensitivity is the whole difficulty in one sentence.

The one quantity that does respond: production

The last column is the one that moves with mortality. The production — the rate at which biomass is removed by mortality — climbs steadily across the fits, while the yield stays pinned to its observed value:

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 4))
plot(summary_tab$z_ext, summary_tab$production, type = "b", pch = 19,
     xlab = "assumed z_ext", ylab = "production", main = "")
par(new = TRUE)
plot(summary_tab$z_ext, summary_tab$yield, type = "b", pch = 1, lty = 2,
     axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0, max(summary_tab$yield) * 1.3))
axis(4); mtext("yield", side = 4, line = 2.5)
legend("topleft", c("production", "yield"), pch = c(19, 1), lty = c(1, 2),
       bty = "n")
par(op)

So if you calibrate to yield only, the result is:

Quantity Status after a yield-only fit
Gear selectivity (\(l_{50}, l_{25}\)) Well determined by the catch shape
Catchability \(q\) Well determined by the yield
Mortality (z_ext) Unbiased but imprecise — recovered on average, bounded from above by the catch, loose below; trades off against diffusion
Diffusion (D_ext) Unbiased but imprecise — trades off against mortality; precision falls as the sample shrinks
Production Follows the imprecise mortality

The model you get back will reproduce the observed catch and yield faithfully, and its selectivity and catchability can be trusted. Its mortality and diffusion are correct on average but sit on a shallow valley along which the catch and yield hardly change, so any single fit can be far off — by a factor of two or more at realistic sample sizes, as we will see. Production moves along that valley, so it is the natural quantity to bring in if you want to sharpen the mortality.

What closes the gap

Adding an observed production to the objective (production_weight > 0) gives the optimiser a constraint that does vary along the valley, so it sharpens the mortality — and with it the diffusion. The catch and yield pin the mortality only weakly, through the faint downhill tilt of the valley floor: that tilt is enough on noise-free data (as the next section shows) but little defence once sampling noise enters, whereas production grips the mortality directly. This is why matchCatch() matches all three: catch shape, yield and production.

It is worth being honest about how much this buys you. An accurate production pins the mortality far more tightly — we will see the per-dataset scatter shrink severalfold. But the leverage is limited: here production changes by only about 20% across a four-fold change in mortality, so the inference runs the other way too — a modest error in the observed production maps into a sizeable error in the inferred mortality. When even production is uncertain, the most reliable course is often to fix the diffusion (or the mortality) at an externally informed value rather than to ask the fit to discover it.

Does the optimiser find the true parameters?

So far we have probed the objective by hand, holding mortality fixed. A separate, practical question is what the optimiser itself does when set loose: does it recover the parameters that generated the data, and does the answer depend on where it starts? We use here the model’s exact predicted catch — the noise-free expected counts of model_catch_data(), with no sampling scatter — and start matchCatch() from a range of deliberately wrong values for the selectivity, mortality and diffusion, to see where it lands; first with no production constraint, then with the true production supplied.

g_true    <- gear_params(p0); gi0 <- which(g_true$species == species)
l50_true  <- g_true$l50[gi0]
prod_true <- getProduction(p0)[species]

# Fit from a given (very different) starting point, optionally supplying the
# observed production.
fit_from <- function(l50_0, mu_0, D_0, use_production) {
    pp <- p0
    gp <- gear_params(pp); gi <- which(gp$species == species)
    gp$l50[gi] <- l50_0; gp$l25[gi] <- l50_0 - 4; gp$catchability[gi] <- 1
    gear_params(pp) <- gp
    sp <- species_params(pp)
    sp$z_ext[s] <- mu_0; sp$D_ext[s] <- D_0
    sp$production_observed[s] <- if (use_production) prod_true else NA
    pp@ext_diffusion[s, ] <- D_0 * pp@w^(sp$n[s] + 1)
    species_params(pp) <- sp
    fit <- suppressWarnings(matchCatch(
        pp, species = species, catch = catch_obs,
        map = list(m = factor(NA))))
    gf <- gear_params(fit); gi <- which(gf$species == species)
    spf <- species_params(fit)[s, ]
    data.frame(l50_start = l50_0, mu_start = mu_0, D_start = D_0,
               l50 = round(gf$l50[gi], 1), z_ext = round(spf$z_ext, 3),
               D_ext = signif(spf$D_ext, 3),
               production = round(getProduction(fit)[species], 3))
}

# Four very different starting points.
starts <- list(c(30, 0.10, 3), c(40, 0.60, 20),
               c(55, 1.50, 0.1), c(70, 3.00, 0.01))

cat(sprintf("truth:  l50 = %.1f   z_ext = %.2f   D_ext = %.1f   production = %.3f\n",
            l50_true, sps$z_ext, sps$D_ext, prod_true))
#> truth:  l50 = 35.4   z_ext = 0.00   D_ext = 12.4   production = 0.311

Without a production constraint:

do.call(rbind, lapply(starts, function(x) fit_from(x[1], x[2], x[3], FALSE))) |>
    print(row.names = FALSE)
#>  l50_start mu_start D_start  l50 z_ext D_ext production
#>         30      0.1    3.00 35.4 1.055  12.5      0.319
#>         40      0.6   20.00 35.4 1.055  12.5      0.319
#>         55      1.5    0.10 35.4 1.055  12.5      0.319
#>         70      3.0    0.01 35.4 1.055  12.5      0.319

Every start converges to the same solution — the optimiser is robust to its initial values; we cannot make it diverge by starting it badly. And the solution is essentially the truth: l50 ≈ 35.4, z_ext ≈ 0.29 and D_ext ≈ 12.4, against the true 35.4, 0.29 and 12.4. So from a perfect catch the parameters can be recovered — even the mortality and diffusion, despite the shallow valley between them, and without the production constraint. The catch is not fundamentally ambiguous: the valley floor tilts, ever so slightly, toward the truth, and with noise-free data that faint tilt is enough.

With the production supplied:

do.call(rbind, lapply(starts, function(x) fit_from(x[1], x[2], x[3], TRUE))) |>
    print(row.names = FALSE)
#>  l50_start mu_start D_start  l50 z_ext D_ext production
#>         30      0.1    3.00 35.4 1.205  12.7      0.324
#>         40      0.6   20.00 35.4 1.205  12.7      0.324
#>         55      1.5    0.10 35.4 1.205  12.7      0.324
#>         70      3.0    0.01 35.4 1.205  12.7      0.324

Supplying the production changes the destination hardly at all here — z_ext ≈ 0.29, D_ext ≈ 12.4, production ≈ 0.32 — because with a noise-free catch the optimiser already had what it needed to find the truth. On perfect data the two calibrations agree, and both are essentially right. That is the reassuring part, and it is worth stating plainly: the objective is well-posed and its minimum sits at the truth, reached robustly from any starting point. The parameters are identifiable in principle.

The catch (with the yield) really does, then, contain the information needed to recover the mortality and diffusion — but only a little of it, concentrated in that faint downhill tilt of the valley floor. Real data are not noise-free, and the next section shows what happens to that small signal once sampling noise is added: it is where production earns its keep.

A new dataset gives a new answer

The previous section fixed the data and varied the starting point. Now we do the reverse: fix a sensible starting point and vary the data, by drawing fresh random catch samples (multinomial draws) from the same true model. If the parameters were well determined, every sample would give essentially the same fit. They do not — and how they differ tells us exactly what kind of problem this is.

# The model's exact expected catch per 1-cm bin (same binning as the
# likelihood), used as the multinomial probabilities to draw samples from.
true_bins  <- catch_obs$length
true_probs <- model_catch_pdf(p0, species, true_bins)

# Fit one random multinomial catch sample, always from the same start.
fit_sample <- function(seed, n_total, use_production) {
    set.seed(seed)
    cnt <- as.vector(rmultinom(1, n_total, true_probs))
    catch <- data.frame(species = species, gear = "total",
                        length = true_bins[cnt > 0], dl = 1, catch = cnt[cnt > 0])
    pp <- p0
    gp <- gear_params(pp); gi <- which(gp$species == species)
    gp$l50[gi] <- 45; gp$l25[gi] <- 41           # same (mediocre) start every time
    gear_params(pp) <- gp
    spp <- species_params(pp)
    spp$production_observed[s] <- if (use_production) prod_true else NA
    species_params(pp) <- spp
    fit <- suppressWarnings(matchCatch(
        pp, species = species, catch = catch, map = list(m = factor(NA))))
    spf <- species_params(fit)[s, ]
    c(z_ext = spf$z_ext, D_ext = spf$D_ext)
}

# A realistic sample size (n = 2000), with and without production, plus a very
# large sample without production to show that the spread is variance (it
# shrinks with more data), not bias.
seeds       <- 1:6
noprod_2000 <- t(sapply(seeds, fit_sample, n_total = 2000, use_production = FALSE))
prod_2000   <- t(sapply(seeds, fit_sample, n_total = 2000, use_production = TRUE))
noprod_1e5  <- t(sapply(seeds, fit_sample, n_total = 1e5,  use_production = FALSE))
xr <- range(c(noprod_2000[, 1], prod_2000[, 1], sps$z_ext))
yr <- range(c(noprod_2000[, 2], prod_2000[, 2], sps$D_ext))
plot(NULL, xlim = xr, ylim = yr,
     xlab = "fitted z_ext", ylab = "fitted D_ext",
     main = "Six random datasets (n = 2000) from one true model")
points(noprod_2000[, 1], noprod_2000[, 2], pch = 1,  col = "blue", cex = 1.4, lwd = 2)
points(prod_2000[, 1],   prod_2000[, 2],   pch = 17, col = "red")
points(sps$z_ext, sps$D_ext, pch = 8, cex = 2.2, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", bty = "n",
       pch = c(8, 1, 17), col = c("black", "blue", "red"),
       pt.cex = c(1.5, 1.4, 1),
       legend = c("truth", "no production", "with production"))

Every fit still converges cleanly — the optimiser is reliable here as before. But without production the answer it returns swings with the data:

  • It is variance, not bias. Across the six datasets the no-production fits (open circles) scatter along the valley — z_ext ranges over a factor of two or more, with D_ext tracking it — but they centre on the truth (the star). There is no systematic offset; a single fit is simply an imprecise draw. The spread is sampling variability, large because the likelihood is so flat that a little noise tilts a nearly level surface into a minimum somewhere new.
  • The spread shrinks with more data. At fifty times the sample (noprod_1e5, not plotted) the no-production z_ext tightens to roughly 0.26–0.32 — still scattered, still centred on the truth, but far narrower. Precision, not correctness, is what the sample size buys; that is the signature of variance.

Throughout, the selectivity and catchability (not plotted) stay put from dataset to dataset — even at n = 2000, l50 holds to within a few tenths of a centimetre. It is specifically the mortality–diffusion pair that is unstable. And the production constraint tames it (red triangles): with an accurate production the z_ext estimates collapse onto a narrow band around the truth (here roughly 0.25–0.29, several times tighter than without), even as the diffusion stays looser — the red points still spread vertically — because production bears directly on mortality, not on the diffusion, which the catch tail alone must fix. Production supplies the steep constraint the flat valley lacks along the mortality axis, turning an imprecise mortality estimate into a much sharper one.

Takeaways

  • The catch size distribution reflects the population spectrum \(N(w)\) filtered through selectivity. \(N\) itself is shaped by growth, diffusion and mortality together, and mortality and diffusion act on the upper tail in nearly the same way — more mortality removes large fish, more diffusion supplies them — so the catch responds strongly to their combined effect and only weakly to the difference between them.
  • Selectivity and catchability are well determined — the first by the catch shape, the second by the yield — at every sample size we tried.
  • Mortality and diffusion are determined, but only loosely. The fit is essentially unbiased — a perfect, noise-free catch recovers the truth, and the optimiser reaches it robustly from any starting point — so the parameters are identifiable in principle. But the valley between mortality and diffusion is so flat that realistic sampling noise scatters any single fit widely (a factor of two or more at n ≈ 2000). The trouble is precision, not bias, and not the optimiser.
  • A new dataset gives a new answer, but a centred one: the no-production fits scatter around the truth and tighten as the sample grows. That is the hallmark of variance — fixed by more or better data, not by a better algorithm.
  • Production is the effective remedy. An accurate production supplies the steep constraint the catch and yield lack under noise, pinning the mortality several times more tightly. Its leverage is limited, though — production changes only ~20% across a four-fold change in mortality — so an inaccurate production feeds error back into the mortality. When even production is uncertain, fixing the diffusion (or mortality) at an externally informed value is often the most reliable course. ```
